blocks.text: ᾿Ανθρακίζων τὲρεβίνθου [anthrakizōn tērebinthou] [col. 47] [II, 584] roasting chickpeas over the coals. And on the second page of the Ecclesiazusae the Scholiast has: Ὑποπίνοντες ἔκοπτον φρυκτοὺς ἐρεβίνθους [hypopinontes ekopton phryktous erebinthous], when they had drunk rather freely, they pounded roasted chickpeas. The Roman writers, too, mention roasted chickpeas more than once. Plautus in the Bacchides, Act 4, Scene 5:
I will make him as roasted as a roasted chickpea.
Nor if the buyer of roasted chickpeas or of nuts approves of something.

Cassian, Collat. 8, ch. 1: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia. Τρωγάλια [trōgalia], that is, sweetmeats. And the Arabs still today call roasted chickpeas قلي [qly] kali, as we have just shown ^{(7)}. Accordingly all the Hebrews, on the passage of Samuel we mentioned, recognize two kinds of kali: the first from grain, the second מקטניות, from legumes, or ממיני קטניות, from kinds of legumes. So Kimchi, R. Levi and R. Esaias on that passage. And R. Selomo describes the second kali thus: וקלי ממינים של קטניות מיבישין אותו בתנור כשהן לחין והם מתוקין לעולם וטוחנין אותן ועושין מהם מאכל שקורין שתית, Kali are kinds of legumes which are dried in the oven while still fresh; they always remain sweet, they are ground, and from them is made a food which they call sethith. This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 38a, where we read that Barzillai the Gileadite sent David תרי מיני שתיתאה, two kinds of sethitha, that is, two kinds of kali. And there the Gloss says: שתיתא תבשיל העשוי מקמח של קליות שייבשין בתנור ויש שעושין אותו מקמח עדשין ולפי שהן מתוקין יותר מדאי נותנים שם חומץ, Sethita is a pottage made from the flour of kali dried in the oven. There are also some who make it from lentil flour, into which, because they are very sweet (that is, insipid), vinegar is poured. And it is true that שתיתא sethitha is said to be made from lentils. For in the tractate Gittin, ch. 7, fol. 70a, in the very text of the Talmud, שתיתא דטלפחי is mentioned, sethitha from lentils. But what is added about vinegar I think is a σφάλμα [sphalma] of the Glossator, who had read somewhere that this pottage is made from lentils וחמצא, and chickpeas, and understood vinegar instead of chickpeas, because in Chaldee חמצא chimtza, chickpea, and חמצא chumtsa, vinegar, are written with the same letters. However that may be, we have amply proved that usnen, or kali, is the chickpea or a kind of chickpea. And we have shown why it is called קלי kali: namely because it is roasted or fried. But اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or rather وشنان [wshnān] vvsnen, as many write it, [II, 585] comes from the verb وشن [wshn], which, of earth, a camel, etc., means to swell and to stand out. Hence the chickpea is rightly called usnen, because of the uneven angles with which it swells and stands out. For it is not round like a pea, but angular and top-shaped ^{(8)}. But why it should be called sparrows' dung or dove's dung is entirely hidden from me. I only know that it is so called. And there is no doubt that the nut Kendem or Gendem is called dove's dung for this very reason, that with its grains or little stones it imitates the form of the chickpea. For it is a granular earth, like chickpeas, as the old translator of Avicenna has it, in the place cited above.
